name: American Sign Language
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: American Sign Language is not in the catalog. All six works with stress in the title are false hits: the saved Glottolog records show each was assigned to ASL [ase] by Glottolog's 'computerized assignment from "manifestation"' on the title word, and they concern English lip kinematics (Cho 2006, two records), Old Germanic alliterative verse (Stanley 1984), the phonetic correlates of word stress across European languages (Dogil & Williams 1999), and lexical stress in Argentine vs Peruvian Spanish (Kim & Nam 2010; Kim 2011 Stony Brook diss., language established from Mücke 2018 p. 78, open CC-BY PDF saved). None bears on ASL. The genuine ASL stress literature is absent from the list of works with stress in the title; Crossref/PubMed lookups identified Wilbur 1999 (Language and Speech 42, DOI 10.1177/00238309990420020501; PubMed abstract saved, full text paywalled) and Wilbur & Schick 1987 (DOI 10.1177/002383098703000402) as the works to acquire.

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern

new_statements.quote: Studies of ASL stress marking reveal that within-sign peak velocity (measured with 3D motion capture) is the primary kinematic marker of stress (Wilbur, 1999b), along with signs being raised in the vertical signing space (Wilbur & Schick, 1987). More relevant to the claim that ASL has a prosodic structure integrated with its syntax is the observation that ASL differs from English, which allows sentential stress to shift to different locations in the sentence depending on the focused or contrasted word. Instead, ASL prefers focus, hence sentence stress, to fall in sentence final position (Wilbur, 1997). In this regard, ASL patterns more like Catalan than like English
new_statements.citation: Wilbur, Ronnie B. 2009. Effects of varying rate of signing on ASL manual signs and nonmanual markers. Language and Speech 52(2-3): 245-285 (NIH author manuscript, PMC2837852).
new_statements.locator: Section 1.1.1 'Stress' (within 1.1 'Prosody in sign languages'), author manuscript; journal pages 245-285, introduction
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Wilbur 2009, Lang Speech 52(2-3): 245-285, NIH author manuscript NIHMS157025). After tag-stripping, the quoted passage is present verbatim at section 1.1.1 "Stress" (under 1.1 "Prosody in sign languages"), from "Studies of ASL stress marking reveal that within-sign peak velocity.. In this regard, ASL patterns more like Catalan than like English"; the section continues "(Vallduvi, 1991, 1992; Wilbur, 1997). Stress will not be considered further in this report." The preceding sentence of 1.1 says rhythm and stress have been studied more than intonation; 1.1.3 adds that above the syllable there is no modality effect in rhythm and stress. So the source gives kinematic stress cues and se…
new_statements.rule_in_words: ASL stress is realised kinematically (higher within-sign peak velocity, signs produced higher in the signing space) and is assigned at the phrase/sentence level: prominence falls on the final sign of the sentence/intonational phrase and cannot be shifted to mark focus (non-plastic, Catalan-type). No positional rule for stress within a (mostly monosyllabic) sign is given; construction-specific word-level statements are base-stressed reduplication (Wilbur) and second-member-stressed compounds (Klima & Bellugi 1979, second-hand).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Wilbur 1999 (Sign Language & Linguistics 2: 217-244, Crossref abstract) identifies final pronouns as exceptions to the phrasal stress-placement regularities.
new_statements.domain_note: Sign language; the positional word-stress typology is inapplicable. The statement concerns stress marking (kinematic cues) and sentence/IP-level prominence; Wilbur's abstract of her 1999 study says lexical stress gets only 'brief mention'. Word-level facts reported first-hand: in reduplicated forms the first occurrence (base) is stressed and copies unstressed (Wilbur 2009 Lang. Sci. 31: 325-342, sec. 5.1, saved); reported second-hand: stress falls on the second member of a compound (Klima & Bellugi 1979 via Sandler 2010 fn. 5, saved). ASL is described as fundamentally monosyllabic, so word-internal stress position rarely arises.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes American Sign Language (ase, amer1248) as used by Deaf signers in the United States; no dialect specified. Sign language: the catalog's positional word-stress categories do not apply; the entry would be a phrase-level/modality note, consistent with the earlier scan_verify S2-outside the catalog's scope.

sources.note: The handout is a semantics lecture note on viewpoint aspect and Aktionsart (sections 1 Viewpoint aspect, 2 Aktionsart, 3 Interaction between viewpoint aspect and Aktionsart) with English, Chinese, Hindi and Slavic examples. A full-text search for stress, accent, prominence, prosody, tone, phonology, 'sign language' and 'ASL' returns nothing relevant (the only hits are 'asleep', 'prominent line of inquiry' and a bibliography title). It does not mention American Sign Language or any sign language; its attachment to [ase] is a Glottolog computerized keyword assignment, not a description of ASL.

sources.note: fn. 5: 'Klima and Bellugi (1979) write that stress falls on the second member of a compound in ASL. In unreduced compounds, in which each member consists of one syllable, this can be seen as evidence for a foot in that language.' Main text: Wilbur's instrumental study shows prominence on the final sign of IPs; fn. 10: 'Little is said here about stress/prominence', deferring to Wilbur 1999, Nespor & Sandler 1999, van der Kooij et al. 2006.

sources.quote: The present focus is on phrasal prominence in ASL. I review the marking of stress and phrase boundaries in ASL, and discuss prominence assignment at the phrasal level, with brief mention of lexical stress. At the kinematic level, there is a modality effect in marking of linguistic prominence but no modality effect with respect to marking phrase position. Of significance is the fact that ASL lacks phrasal prominence plasticity, that is the ability to move prominence to mark focus in a sentence location other than phrase final.
sources.note: The primary instrumental study of ASL stress; abstract promises the review of stress marking, phrasal prominence assignment and a 'brief mention of lexical stress' — the direct first-hand statement on word-level stress would be here.
